questions.question: A 34-year-old man is evaluated 2 days after being struck on the side of the head with an open hand. He reports muffled hearing and fullness in the right ear but denies vertigo or tinnitus. Otoscopy shows a 4-mm central perforation of the right tympanic membrane with dried blood along its edges; the external canal is patent. Audiometry demonstrates a 30-dB air-bone gap on the right with normal bone conduction thresholds bilaterally. Which of the following best explains his hearing deficit?

answers.A: Blockage of the external auditory canal by inflammatory debris
answers.B: Fixation of the stapes footplate within the oval window
answers.C: Loss of the impedance-matching function of the middle ear
answers.D: Necrosis of outer hair cells along the basal turn of the cochlea
answers.E: Rupture of the round window membrane with leakage of perilymph

explanations.A: Canal obstruction by cerumen or debris also causes a conductive loss, but his canal is patent and the perforation is directly visualized.
explanations.B: Stapes fixation is the mechanism of otosclerosis, which produces a conductive loss with a normal, intact tympanic membrane.
explanations.C: The large tympanic membrane surface relative to the oval window plus the ossicular lever normally add roughly 30 dB to overcome the air-to-fluid impedance mismatch, and perforation abolishes this gain while leaving cochlear function intact.
explanations.D: Basal-turn outer hair cell loss produces a high-frequency sensorineural pattern with reduced bone conduction, not an air-bone gap.
explanations.E: A perilymphatic fistula at the round window causes sensorineural hearing loss with vertigo, not an isolated air-bone gap.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man who has worked on a stamping-press factory floor for 25 years without hearing protection reports several years of difficulty understanding conversation, worse in crowded rooms. Otoscopy shows normal tympanic membranes bilaterally, and the Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction in both ears. Pure-tone audiometry results are shown. Injury to hair cells in which of the following locations best accounts for this audiogram?

answers.A: Base of the cochlea, near the oval window
answers.B: Crista ampullaris of the posterior semicircular canal
answers.C: Helicotrema at the apex of the cochlear duct
answers.D: Macula of the saccule within the vestibule
answers.E: Middle turn of the cochlea, near the modiolus

explanations.A: The basilar membrane is tonotopically organized so that high frequencies produce maximal displacement at the stiff, narrow base, which is why noise exposure classically produces a 4000-Hz notch.
explanations.B: The crista ampullaris transduces angular acceleration for balance and has no role in frequency-specific hearing thresholds.
explanations.C: The apex near the helicotrema encodes low frequencies, which are the best-preserved frequencies on this audiogram.
explanations.D: The saccular macula detects vertical linear acceleration and would produce vestibular rather than auditory symptoms if injured.
explanations.E: The middle turn encodes mid frequencies (roughly 1000-2000 Hz), which show only minimal threshold elevation here.

questions.question: Investigators selectively ablate the motor protein prestin in the outer hair cells of adult mice. Inner hair cells, the tectorial membrane, the spiral ganglion, and the endocochlear potential generated by the stria vascularis are all confirmed to be intact. Auditory brainstem responses show a 40-dB elevation of thresholds with markedly broadened frequency tuning curves. Which normal cochlear function has most likely been lost?

answers.A: Conversion of endolymph displacement into afferent nerve impulses
answers.B: Equalization of air pressure across the tympanic membrane
answers.C: Generation of the endocochlear potential by the stria vascularis
answers.D: Mechanical amplification and sharpening of basilar membrane tuning
answers.E: Transduction of angular head acceleration by the crista ampullaris

explanations.A: Conversion of mechanical displacement into afferent firing is the job of the single row of inner hair cells, which are explicitly preserved in this model.
explanations.B: Pressure equalization is performed by the eustachian tube in the middle ear and is unrelated to cochlear hair cell proteins.
explanations.C: The endocochlear potential is generated by the stria vascularis and is stated to be intact in these animals.
explanations.D: The three rows of outer hair cells use prestin-driven electromotility to amplify and sharply tune basilar membrane motion, so their loss raises thresholds and broadens tuning curves.
explanations.E: Angular acceleration is transduced by vestibular hair cells in the crista ampullaris, which are not cochlear outer hair cells.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman participates in a study of vestibular function. She is seated fully upright with her eyes closed inside an enclosed elevator that accelerates upward at a constant rate; she accurately reports the direction and onset of the vertical motion. Her head is held immobile throughout and there is no rotation in any plane. Which receptor organ is chiefly responsible for detecting this stimulus?

answers.A: Crista ampullaris of the lateral semicircular canal
answers.B: Macula of the saccule
answers.C: Macula of the utricle
answers.D: Organ of Corti at the cochlear base
answers.E: Spiral ganglion within the modiolus

explanations.A: The lateral canal crista detects angular (rotational) acceleration in the horizontal plane, and the head is held immobile without rotation.
explanations.B: The saccular macula is oriented vertically so that its otoconia-weighted otolithic membrane shears the stereocilia during vertical linear acceleration.
explanations.C: The utricular macula lies horizontally and detects horizontal linear acceleration and static head tilt rather than vertical motion.
explanations.D: The organ of Corti transduces sound, not head motion, and its basal turn encodes high-frequency hearing.
explanations.E: The spiral ganglion contains the cell bodies of cochlear afferents and is a relay for auditory rather than vestibular input.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has had five episodes of acute otitis media in the past 12 months. His parents report loud snoring, chronic mouth breathing, and hyponasal speech. Otoscopy today shows a dull, retracted right tympanic membrane with an air-fluid level. A lateral nasopharyngeal radiograph shows a markedly enlarged adenoid pad narrowing the nasopharyngeal airway. Which mechanism best explains his recurrent middle ear infections?

answers.A: Ciliary dysfunction impairing clearance of middle ear secretions
answers.B: Direct inoculation of the middle ear through the external canal
answers.C: Hematogenous seeding of the mastoid air cells from the nasopharynx
answers.D: Immunoglobulin A deficiency with impaired mucosal defense
answers.E: Obstruction of the eustachian tube with poor ventilation

explanations.A: Primary ciliary dyskinesia causes recurrent otitis but is typically accompanied by situs abnormalities, bronchiectasis, and chronic sinopulmonary disease.
explanations.B: The intact tympanic membrane separates the canal from the middle ear, so canal organisms cause otitis externa rather than otitis media.
explanations.C: Middle ear and mastoid infection in this setting ascends through the eustachian tube from the nasopharynx rather than arriving through the bloodstream.
explanations.D: Selective IgA deficiency can cause recurrent mucosal infections but would not explain the obstructing adenoid pad and airway symptoms.
explanations.E: Adenoid hypertrophy blocks the nasopharyngeal orifice of the eustachian tube, so the middle ear cannot ventilate or drain and nasopharyngeal pathogens are retained.

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman consistently develops a dry, hacking cough whenever the physician removes cerumen from her left external auditory canal with a curette. The cough begins within seconds of instrumentation and stops as soon as the instrument is withdrawn. She has no pulmonary symptoms otherwise, and chest examination and chest radiograph are normal. Stimulation of which nerve best explains this reflex?

answers.A: Auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of CN V3
answers.B: Chorda tympani, a branch of CN VII
answers.C: Glossopharyngeal nerve, via its tympanic branch
answers.D: Vagus nerve, via its auricular branch
answers.E: Vestibulocochlear nerve, via its cochlear division

explanations.A: The auriculotemporal nerve supplies sensation to the anterior canal and tympanic membrane but does not carry afferents into the cough reflex arc.
explanations.B: The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior tongue and parasympathetic fibers, and it does not mediate a cough reflex.
explanations.C: The tympanic branch of CN IX (Jacobson nerve) innervates the middle ear mucosa rather than the external canal skin.
explanations.D: The auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold nerve) supplies part of the external canal, so mechanical stimulation there triggers the vagally mediated cough reflex.
explanations.E: CN VIII carries only special sensory hearing and balance afferents and mediates no somatic reflexes.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman reports 18 months of progressive right-sided hearing loss with tinnitus and mild unsteadiness. Audiometry shows right sensorineural hearing loss with speech discrimination far worse than predicted by her pure-tone thresholds. MRI shows a 2.2-cm enhancing mass centered at the right cerebellopontine angle that extends into and widens the internal acoustic meatus. Which additional cranial nerve is most likely to be compromised as the lesion expands within this canal?

answers.A: Abducens nerve
answers.B: Facial nerve
answers.C: Glossopharyngeal nerve
answers.D: Hypoglossal nerve
answers.E: Oculomotor nerve

explanations.A: CN VI exits through the superior orbital fissure and is affected by petrous apex lesions rather than by tumor within the internal acoustic meatus.
explanations.B: The facial nerve traverses the internal acoustic meatus alongside CN VIII, so an intracanalicular schwannoma compresses it and can cause ipsilateral facial weakness.
explanations.C: CN IX leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and is spared by a lesion confined to the internal acoustic meatus.
explanations.D: CN XII exits via the hypoglossal canal well inferior and medial to the internal acoustic meatus.
explanations.E: CN III exits through the superior orbital fissure and is remote from the cerebellopontine angle.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man is evaluated after a small infarct restricted to the caudal pontine tegmentum. Pure-tone audiometry is normal bilaterally and he understands conversational speech without difficulty. However, when a sound is presented from a random position around him with his eyes closed, he cannot identify which side of the room it came from. Injury to which structure best explains this deficit?

answers.A: Dorsal cochlear nucleus
answers.B: Inferior colliculus
answers.C: Medial geniculate nucleus
answers.D: Superior olivary complex
answers.E: Transverse temporal gyrus

explanations.A: The dorsal cochlear nucleus is the first central relay for monaural input and lies in the rostral medulla, not the caudal pontine tegmentum.
explanations.B: The inferior colliculus is a midbrain relay that integrates ascending auditory input, and lesions there do not selectively abolish horizontal localization.
explanations.C: The medial geniculate nucleus is the thalamic auditory relay and is located far from the caudal pons.
explanations.D: The superior olivary complex in the caudal pons is the first site of binaural convergence and computes interaural time and intensity differences used for sound localization.
explanations.E: The transverse temporal gyri house primary auditory cortex, and unilateral lesions there impair perception rather than binaural localization at this level.

questions.question: A 63-year-old right-handed woman is evaluated after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. She speaks fluently with normal rate and prosody but produces frequent nonsense words, and she cannot follow simple spoken commands or repeat phrases. She startles and turns appropriately toward unexpected sounds, and pure-tone audiometry is normal in both ears. Which region is most likely damaged?

answers.A: Association cortex of the dominant superior temporal gyrus
answers.B: Inferior colliculus of the contralateral midbrain tegmentum
answers.C: Medial geniculate nucleus of the posteromedial thalamus
answers.D: Primary auditory cortex of the transverse temporal gyri
answers.E: Ventral cochlear nucleus of the rostral medulla

explanations.A: Auditory association cortex in the dominant superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22, Wernicke area) supports sound recognition and language comprehension, so its loss yields fluent speech without meaning.
explanations.B: An inferior colliculus lesion would degrade auditory relay function but not selectively destroy language comprehension with preserved fluency.
explanations.C: Medial geniculate injury interrupts thalamocortical auditory transmission and would be expected to alter audiometric thresholds or cortical responsiveness.
explanations.D: Primary auditory cortex (areas 41 and 42) mediates conscious sound perception, and bilateral loss causes cortical deafness rather than a comprehension aphasia.
explanations.E: Cochlear nucleus injury produces ipsilateral hearing loss on audiometry, which is normal in this patient.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl is brought for a kindergarten readiness well-child visit. She was born at term, has no chronic medical problems, and her hearing and vision screens are normal. Her parents ask whether her behavior and language are on track for her age. Which of the following findings would be most consistent with normal development for a 5-year-old?

answers.A: Copies a circle and engages mainly in associative play
answers.B: Follows rules in group games and tells a connected story
answers.C: Names four colors and draws a person with a head and limbs
answers.D: Speaks in two-word phrases that are about half intelligible
answers.E: Uses three-word sentences that are about 75% intelligible

explanations.A: Copying a circle and associative play are typical of a 3-year-old and would be developmentally behind at age 5.
explanations.B: By age 5 children follow rules and take turns in group games, count to 10, write some letters, and tell fully intelligible connected stories.
explanations.C: Naming colors, drawing a person, and cooperative play describe the 4-year-old milestone set.
explanations.D: Two-word phrases that are 50% intelligible are expected at about 2 years of age.
explanations.E: Three-word sentences with 75% intelligibility correspond to the 3-year-old milestone.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis reports that the room appears to bounce whenever she walks or turns her head. Her hearing is normal, and there is no spinning sensation at rest. On examination, rapid passive rotation of her head fails to produce an equal and opposite conjugate eye movement, and she must stop and stand still to read a sign. Impairment of which pathway best explains her oscillopsia?

answers.A: Brachium of the inferior colliculus
answers.B: Corticospinal tract
answers.C: Inferior cerebellar peduncle
answers.D: Lateral vestibulospinal tract
answers.E: Medial longitudinal fasciculus

explanations.A: The brachium of the inferior colliculus carries auditory fibers to the medial geniculate and has no oculomotor function.
explanations.B: The corticospinal tract mediates voluntary limb movement, and its injury produces weakness and spasticity rather than gaze instability.
explanations.C: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries vestibulocerebellar fibers to the flocculonodular lobe and modulates rather than executes the reflex eye movement.
explanations.D: The lateral vestibulospinal tract drives antigravity extensor tone for posture, not compensatory eye movements.
explanations.E: The vestibulo-ocular reflex ascends from the vestibular nuclei in the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the nuclei of CN III, IV, and VI, and its disruption prevents gaze stabilization and causes oscillopsia.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy is referred because his teacher reports that he "never pays attention" in class. He rarely makes eye contact, plays alone at recess, and lines his toy cars in rows for long stretches. He repeats phrases from videos verbatim and has severe tantrums when the classroom routine changes. His parents note he can focus for 45 minutes at a time on his train collection. He is not defiant and does not fidget or leave his seat. Which diagnosis best accounts for these findings?

answers.A: Autism spectrum disorder
answers.B: Conduct disorder
answers.C: Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
answers.D: Oppositional defiant disorder
answers.E: Predominantly inattentive ADHD

explanations.A: Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity plus restricted, repetitive behaviors, echolalia, insistence on sameness, and intensely fixated interests define autism spectrum disorder and mimic inattention in the classroom.
explanations.B: Conduct disorder requires repetitive violation of the rights of others such as aggression, property destruction, deceitfulness, or serious rule violations, none of which are present.
explanations.C: DMDD requires a persistently angry or irritable baseline mood with severe temper outbursts at least three times weekly, whereas his outbursts are tied specifically to routine changes.
explanations.D: ODD is characterized by deliberate defiance, arguing with authority, and vindictiveness, and this boy is described as not defiant.
explanations.E: ADHD attention is sidetracked by unimportant external stimuli, which is inconsistent with his sustained 45-minute focus and does not explain the echolalia or social deficits.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man reports 3 days of decreased hearing and fullness in the left ear that began after swimming at a lake. He has no ear pain, vertigo, tinnitus, or drainage, and no pain with tragal pressure. His own voice sounds normal in volume to him, and he notes that he actually hears conversation better in a noisy room. Tuning fork testing at 512 Hz gives the results shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Acoustic neuroma of the left cerebellopontine angle
answers.B: Cerumen impaction of the left external auditory canal
answers.C: Noise-induced sensorineural hearing loss of the left cochlea
answers.D: Ototoxic cochlear injury from intravenous gentamicin
answers.E: Presbycusis with asymmetric high-frequency loss

explanations.A: An acoustic neuroma produces sensorineural loss with the Weber lateralizing away from the affected ear and air conduction remaining greater than bone conduction.
explanations.B: Weber lateralizing to the affected ear with bone conduction greater than air conduction on that side defines a conductive loss, and cerumen swelling after water exposure with a normal-volume voice and better hearing in noise fits an external canal obstruction.
explanations.C: Noise-induced loss is sensorineural, typically bilateral, and would lateralize the Weber to the better ear.
explanations.D: Aminoglycoside ototoxicity damages cochlear hair cells and causes a sensorineural pattern with preserved air-over-bone conduction.
explanations.E: Presbycusis is a sensorineural high-frequency loss in which speech understanding worsens rather than improves in noisy environments.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman reports 6 months of progressive right-sided hearing loss with constant high-pitched tinnitus. She says sounds seem distorted and that she does much worse understanding speech in noisy restaurants; her family says she has begun speaking loudly. Otoscopy shows normal external canals and tympanic membranes bilaterally. Tuning fork testing gives the results shown. Which is the most likely site of the lesion?

answers.A: External auditory canal on the right
answers.B: Ossicular chain of the right middle ear
answers.C: Round window membrane on the right
answers.D: Tympanic membrane on the right
answers.E: Vestibulocochlear nerve on the right

explanations.A: Canal obstruction produces a conductive pattern with bone conduction exceeding air conduction and the Weber lateralizing to the affected side.
explanations.B: Ossicular disruption or fixation causes an air-bone gap on the right, which is not present here.
explanations.C: A round window lesion such as a perilymphatic fistula typically causes abrupt hearing loss with vertigo after barotrauma rather than an insidious 6-month course.
explanations.D: The tympanic membranes are visualized and normal, and membrane pathology would produce a conductive pattern.
explanations.E: Weber lateralizing away from the affected ear with air conduction still exceeding bone conduction indicates a right sensorineural loss, and the disproportionate discrimination loss with loud voice and worsening in noise localizes to the cochlea or CN VIII.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman reports 2 years of progressive bilateral hearing loss that noticeably worsened during her recent pregnancy. She reports mild tinnitus but no vertigo, otorrhea, or ear pain, and she hears better in noisy environments while speaking at a normal volume. Her mother and maternal uncle both required hearing aids in their thirties. Otoscopy shows normal, mobile tympanic membranes bilaterally, and the Rinne test shows bone conduction greater than air conduction in both ears. Which pathologic process best explains her hearing loss?

answers.A: Accumulation of keratin debris eroding the ossicular chain
answers.B: Distention of the endolymphatic compartment of the cochlear duct
answers.C: Loss of cochlear hair cells from cumulative noise exposure
answers.D: Serous effusion in the middle ear from eustachian tube dysfunction
answers.E: Vascular spongy bone replacing lamellar bone at the oval window

explanations.A: Keratin accumulation describes cholesteatoma, which causes chronic foul otorrhea and a visible retraction pocket or pearly mass rather than normal tympanic membranes.
explanations.B: Endolymphatic hydrops underlies Meniere disease, which causes episodic vertigo with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, not a bilateral conductive loss.
explanations.C: Noise-induced injury is sensorineural, so air conduction would still exceed bone conduction and hearing would worsen in noise.
explanations.D: A middle ear effusion produces a dull, retracted, immobile tympanic membrane, whereas hers are normal and mobile.
explanations.E: Otosclerosis is an autosomal dominant disorder of the otic capsule in which lamellar bone is replaced by vascular spongy bone at the oval window, fixing the stapes footplate and producing a progressive conductive loss behind a normal membrane.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being thrown from his bicycle onto pavement; he had a brief loss of consciousness and now has a headache. He has clear fluid dripping from the right nostril that tests positive for beta-2 transferrin, and there is bruising behind the right ear. A lateral skull radiograph shows no visible fracture line but demonstrates an air-fluid level within the sphenoid sinus. Which of the following best explains this radiographic finding?

answers.A: Acute bacterial sphenoid sinusitis with purulent secretions
answers.B: Depressed fracture of the parietal bone with overlapping edges
answers.C: Fracture of the skull base with hemorrhage into the sinus
answers.D: Normal pneumatization variant of the sphenoid sinus
answers.E: Overlying scalp hematoma projecting over the sinus

explanations.A: Sinusitis would cause a subacute course with fever, facial pain, and purulent nasal discharge rather than acute posttraumatic clear rhinorrhea.
explanations.B: A depressed fracture appears on radiograph as white lines of increased density from overlapping bone fragments, which are absent here.
explanations.C: An air-fluid level in the sphenoid sinus after head trauma indicates blood or cerebrospinal fluid tracking from a basal skull fracture, and a clear fracture line often is not visible on plain film.
explanations.D: Normal pneumatization yields a uniformly aerated, lucent sinus without a dependent fluid level.
explanations.E: A scalp hematoma is a soft-tissue density outside the calvarium and does not create a dependent fluid level inside an air-filled sinus.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy is receiving multiagent chemotherapy for osteosarcoma of the distal femur. After his third cycle he reports constant ringing in both ears and difficulty hearing his teacher from across the classroom. His tympanic membranes are normal and mobile, and there is no ear pain or drainage. Audiometry shows new symmetric bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with normal thresholds below 2000 Hz. Which agent in his regimen is most likely responsible?

answers.A: Bleomycin
answers.B: Cisplatin
answers.C: Doxorubicin
answers.D: Methotrexate
answers.E: Vincristine

explanations.A: Bleomycin causes dose-dependent pulmonary fibrosis rather than cochlear injury.
explanations.B: Platinum-based agents are classically ototoxic, destroying outer hair cells at the cochlear base and producing bilateral high-frequency sensorineural loss with tinnitus.
explanations.C: Doxorubicin causes dilated cardiomyopathy through free-radical myocardial injury, not hearing loss.
explanations.D: Methotrexate toxicity manifests as mucositis, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, and nephrotoxicity.
explanations.E: Vincristine causes a peripheral axonal neuropathy with areflexia and paresthesias rather than cochlear damage.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman reports 2 weeks of brief spinning episodes that last less than a minute and are triggered by rolling over in bed and by tilting her head back to reach a high shelf. She is entirely asymptomatic between episodes and has no hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness, dysarthria, or diplopia. Neurologic examination is normal. The right Dix-Hallpike maneuver reproduces her vertigo after a 5-second latency with transient upbeating-torsional nystagmus that fatigues on repeat testing. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
answers.B: Meniere disease with endolymphatic hydrops
answers.C: Orthostatic hypotension from volume depletion
answers.D: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency with brainstem ischemia
answers.E: Vestibular neuritis following a viral infection

explanations.A: Brief positionally triggered vertigo with a latency-onset, fatigable upbeating-torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike is the signature of otoconial debris within the posterior semicircular canal.
explanations.B: Meniere disease produces vertigo lasting hours accompanied by aural fullness, roaring tinnitus, and fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss.
explanations.C: Orthostatic hypotension causes lightheadedness and dimmed vision seconds after standing without any illusion of spinning or positional nystagmus.
explanations.D: Vertebrobasilar ischemia typically produces vertigo with accompanying brainstem signs such as dysarthria, diplopia, or dysmetria.
explanations.E: Vestibular neuritis causes continuous vertigo lasting days with persistent unidirectional nystagmus, not brief positional attacks.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man has had five episodes over 8 months of severe spinning vertigo with nausea, each lasting 2 to 3 hours. Every attack is preceded by a sensation of fullness and a low-pitched roaring tinnitus in the left ear. Between episodes his neurologic examination and gait are normal, and there is no dysarthria, diplopia, or dysmetria. Audiometry performed between attacks shows fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss on the left. Which mechanism best explains his presentation?

answers.A: Debris within the posterior semicircular canal
answers.B: Demyelination at the vestibular nerve root entry zone
answers.C: Distention of the endolymphatic space from impaired resorption
answers.D: Ischemia of the lateral medulla from vertebral artery occlusion
answers.E: Viral inflammation of the vestibular portion of CN VIII

explanations.A: Canalith debris causes vertigo lasting seconds with positional triggers and no hearing symptoms.
explanations.B: Root entry zone demyelination in multiple sclerosis is a central cause that would be accompanied by other neurologic signs and would not produce fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss.
explanations.C: Meniere disease results from endolymphatic hydrops, in which distention of the endolymphatic compartment produces episodic vertigo lasting hours with aural fullness, roaring tinnitus, and fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss.
explanations.D: Lateral medullary infarction produces sudden persistent vertigo with crossed sensory loss, Horner syndrome, and dysphagia rather than recurrent stereotyped attacks.
explanations.E: Vestibular neuritis is a single prolonged attack lasting days and characteristically spares hearing.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman has had continuous vertigo, nausea, and unsteadiness for 2 days that began several days after an upper respiratory infection. Symptoms are constant but worsen with head movement, and she can walk with one-person assistance. She reports no hearing change, dysarthria, dysphagia, diplopia, or limb weakness. Bedside vestibular testing shows the findings below. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
table: Horizontal, unidirectional, right-beating in all gaze positions
Corrective saccade with leftward head thrust

answers.A: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
answers.B: Cerebellar infarction in the PICA territory
answers.C: Meniere disease with endolymphatic hydrops
answers.D: Vestibular neuritis, left superior division
answers.E: Wallenberg lateral medullary syndrome

explanations.A: BPPV produces brief positionally triggered attacks, not continuous vertigo lasting days with spontaneous nystagmus.
explanations.B: A cerebellar stroke gives a normal head impulse test with direction-changing nystagmus and often an inability to stand unassisted.
explanations.C: Meniere attacks last hours and are accompanied by aural fullness, tinnitus, and fluctuating hearing loss, whereas her audiometry is normal.
explanations.D: An abnormal head impulse test with corrective saccade, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus, and absent skew is the peripheral pattern, and a postviral course with preserved hearing indicates vestibular neuritis rather than labyrinthitis.
explanations.E: Lateral medullary syndrome adds crossed sensory loss, Horner syndrome, hoarseness, and dysphagia, all of which are absent.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation not taking anticoagulation has had 6 hours of continuous vertigo with vomiting. He cannot stand without falling toward the left even with assistance. He denies hearing loss or tinnitus, and the external canals and tympanic membranes are normal. Bedside vestibular testing shows the findings below. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
table: Direction-changing: right-beating on right gaze, left-beating on left gaze
Normal; no corrective saccade in either direction

answers.A: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
answers.B: Bilateral vestibulopathy from aminoglycoside toxicity
answers.C: Cerebellar infarction in the PICA territory
answers.D: Meniere disease with endolymphatic hydrops
answers.E: Vestibular neuritis of the right vestibular nerve

explanations.A: BPPV causes brief fatigable positional vertigo with a normal neurologic examination and preserved standing balance.
explanations.B: Aminoglycoside vestibulotoxicity presents with chronic oscillopsia and gait instability rather than acute vertigo with skew deviation.
explanations.C: A normal head impulse test combined with direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, skew deviation, and inability to stand is the central pattern, and atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation makes posterior circulation cardioembolic infarction most likely.
explanations.D: Meniere attacks last hours with aural fullness, tinnitus, and hearing loss, and they do not produce skew deviation.
explanations.E: Vestibular neuritis would produce an abnormal head impulse test with unidirectional nystagmus and no skew.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman reports recurrent episodes of lightheadedness with graying and dimming of her vision that begin within seconds of standing and resolve when she sits down. She also describes an aching pain across the back of her neck and shoulders when she is upright for long periods. She started hydrochlorothiazide 3 weeks ago. She denies any spinning sensation, hearing change, tinnitus, or nausea, and there is no nystagmus. Vital signs are shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
answers.B: Disequilibrium from peripheral neuropathy
answers.C: Meniere disease
answers.D: Orthostatic hypotension
answers.E: Vestibular neuritis

explanations.A: BPPV causes a true illusion of spinning triggered by head position changes rather than by upright posture, with characteristic positional nystagmus.
explanations.B: Disequilibrium is a sense of being off balance while walking, without lightheadedness, visual dimming, or a postural blood pressure drop.
explanations.C: Meniere disease produces vertigo lasting hours with aural fullness, tinnitus, and hearing loss, none of which are present.
explanations.D: Lightheadedness with visual dimming within seconds of standing, a documented postural drop of more than 20 mm Hg systolic after starting a diuretic, and coat-hanger neck and shoulder pain identify systemic hypotension causing cerebral hypoperfusion.
explanations.E: Vestibular neuritis causes continuous vertigo lasting days with spontaneous nystagmus and an abnormal head impulse test.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with 15 years of type 2 diabetes reports feeling unsteady on his feet, particularly when walking down a dim hallway at night or turning corners. He denies any sensation of spinning, lightheadedness, visual dimming, nausea, tinnitus, or hearing change. Examination shows a wide-based cautious gait, absent vibration and joint position sense at both great toes, and a positive Romberg sign. There is no nystagmus, and orthostatic vital signs are normal. Which best explains his symptoms?

answers.A: Disequilibrium from impaired proprioceptive input
answers.B: Orthostatic presyncope from intravascular volume depletion
answers.C: Peripheral vertigo from semicircular canal debris
answers.D: Presyncope from an intermittent cardiac arrhythmia
answers.E: Vertigo from inflammation of the vestibular nerve

explanations.A: Disequilibrium is a sense of imbalance without any illusion of motion, and loss of proprioceptive input from diabetic neuropathy produces a wide-based gait, positive Romberg, and symptoms that worsen in the dark when visual compensation is lost.
explanations.B: Presyncope from volume depletion produces lightheadedness and dimmed vision on standing with a documented orthostatic blood pressure drop, which is absent here.
explanations.C: Canalith debris causes brief spinning episodes provoked by specific head positions, and this patient explicitly denies any spinning.
explanations.D: An arrhythmia causes abrupt lightheadedness or syncope independent of gait and lighting conditions.
explanations.E: Vestibular nerve inflammation causes continuous vertigo with nystagmus and nausea, none of which are present.

questions.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought in with 2 days of fever and tugging at his right ear, beginning 4 days after the onset of rhinorrhea and cough. He is fussy but consolable and drinking normally. The right auricle is in normal position, and there is no postauricular swelling, erythema, or tenderness. Otoscopy shows a bulging, opaque, erythematous right tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex and reduced mobility on pneumatic insufflation. Vital signs are shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Acute mastoiditis
answers.B: Acute otitis externa
answers.C: Acute otitis media
answers.D: Cholesteatoma with ossicular erosion
answers.E: Otitis media with effusion

explanations.A: Mastoiditis requires postauricular tenderness, swelling, and a protruding auricle, all of which are explicitly absent.
explanations.B: Otitis externa causes pain on tragal pressure or auricular traction with an inflamed canal and a normal tympanic membrane.
explanations.C: A post-viral course with acute deep otalgia, fever, and a bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane reflects eustachian tube dysfunction with bacterial infection of retained middle ear fluid.
explanations.D: Cholesteatoma presents with chronic painless foul otorrhea, progressive conductive hearing loss, and a retraction pocket or pearly mass rather than acute fever.
explanations.E: Otitis media with effusion shows a dull, retracted or neutral membrane with fluid but without the fever, pain, and erythema of acute infection.

questions.question: A 16-year-old competitive swimmer has 3 days of right ear pain and intense itching. Pain is reproduced by pressing on the tragus and by pulling upward on the auricle. The external canal is erythematous, edematous, and filled with moist debris; the visible portion of the tympanic membrane is normal and mobile. He is afebrile, and there is no postauricular tenderness. Which organism is the most likely cause?

answers.A: Haemophilus influenzae
answers.B: Moraxella catarrhalis
answers.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
answers.D: Staphylococcus aureus
answers.E: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanations.A: Nontypeable H. influenzae is a leading cause of acute otitis media reached via the eustachian tube, not of external canal infection.
explanations.B: M. catarrhalis colonizes the upper respiratory tract and causes otitis media following viral upper respiratory infection.
explanations.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa accounts for roughly 40% of otitis externa, thriving in the moist canal after swimming causes skin barrier breakdown.
explanations.D: S. aureus is the second most common otitis externa pathogen but is less frequent than Pseudomonas, particularly in swimmers.
explanations.E: S. pneumoniae is the leading cause of acute otitis media and mastoiditis rather than of external canal disease.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has 3 weeks of severe left ear pain and drainage that has not improved despite topical antibiotic drops. The pain wakes him at night and is far worse than his examination would suggest. Otoscopy shows granulation tissue at the bone-cartilage junction of the canal floor. He has new left-sided facial weakness involving the forehead. Laboratory studies are shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Acute mastoiditis with subperiosteal abscess
answers.B: Bell palsy
answers.C: Cholesteatoma with facial nerve erosion
answers.D: Herpes zoster oticus
answers.E: Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa

explanations.A: Mastoiditis produces postauricular swelling and tenderness with a protruding auricle rather than canal granulation tissue.
explanations.B: Bell palsy is an isolated idiopathic facial paresis without severe otalgia, otorrhea, canal granulation, or a markedly elevated sedimentation rate.
explanations.C: Cholesteatoma causes chronic painless otorrhea with a pearly retraction pocket mass and progressive conductive hearing loss, not intense pain with granulation at the bone-cartilage junction.
explanations.D: Ramsay Hunt syndrome causes facial palsy with vesicles in the canal and on the auricle, which are absent here.
explanations.E: Necrotizing otitis externa is a Pseudomonas skull base osteomyelitis of diabetic and immunocompromised patients, marked by pain out of proportion, canal granulation tissue, a very high sedimentation rate, and cranial nerve palsies.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy has 2 years of intermittent painless, foul-smelling drainage from the left ear with progressively worsening hearing on that side. The Rinne test shows bone conduction greater than air conduction on the left, and the Weber lateralizes to the left. Otoscopy reveals a retraction pocket in the pars flaccida containing a pearly white mass. CT shows erosion of the long process of the incus. The lesion is excised. Which finding is most likely on histologic examination?

answers.A: Caseating granulomas containing acid-fast bacilli
answers.B: Dilated endolymphatic sac lined by flattened epithelium
answers.C: Fibrovascular polyp with dense neutrophilic exudate
answers.D: Keratinizing squamous epithelium with keratin debris
answers.E: Vascular spongy bone replacing lamellar otic capsule bone

explanations.A: Caseating granulomas indicate tuberculous otitis media, which classically causes multiple painless perforations rather than a pars flaccida retraction pocket with a pearly mass.
explanations.B: A dilated endolymphatic compartment describes the hydrops of Meniere disease, which causes episodic vertigo and sensorineural loss.
explanations.C: An inflammatory aural polyp may accompany chronic otitis media but does not explain the pearly retraction pocket mass with ossicular erosion.
explanations.D: Cholesteatoma is a cystic collection of keratinizing squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid whose trapped desquamated keratin drives chronic inflammation and ossicular erosion.
explanations.E: Vascular spongy bone at the oval window is the lesion of otosclerosis, which produces conductive loss behind a normal tympanic membrane without otorrhea.

questions.question: A 3-year-old girl completed a course of amoxicillin for acute otitis media 2 weeks ago but has had persistent right ear pain, drainage, and fever. She now has swelling behind the right ear. On examination the retroauricular sulcus is obliterated, the auricle is displaced downward and outward, and the postauricular area is warm, erythematous, and exquisitely tender. Otoscopy shows a bulging, erythematous right tympanic membrane. Laboratory studies are shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Acute mastoiditis with subperiosteal abscess
answers.B: Bezold abscess of the deep neck spaces
answers.C: Cervical lymphadenitis of the upper neck nodes
answers.D: Parotitis involving the right parotid gland
answers.E: Preauricular cellulitis of the facial skin

explanations.A: Persistent otitis media beyond 2 weeks with postauricular swelling, loss of the retroauricular sulcus, and an auricle protruding down and out indicates coalescent mastoiditis that has eroded the lateral mastoid cortex beneath the periosteum.
explanations.B: A Bezold abscess results from erosion through the mastoid tip and presents as a neck mass deep to the sternocleidomastoid rather than swelling directly behind the ear.
explanations.C: Cervical lymphadenitis produces tender nodes along the neck without obliteration of the retroauricular sulcus or auricular displacement.
explanations.D: Parotitis causes swelling anterior and inferior to the ear that lifts the earlobe outward, with tenderness over the parotid gland.
explanations.E: Preauricular cellulitis involves the skin anterior to the tragus and would not displace the auricle or efface the postauricular sulcus.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy has had purulent drainage from the right ear for 3 weeks despite two courses of oral antibiotics. He now reports deep right-sided retro-orbital and facial pain along with horizontal double vision that worsens on right gaze. Examination shows failure of right eye abduction with a reactive pupil, no ptosis, and normal pupillary responses. There is no postauricular swelling and no meningismus. Which complication best explains his findings?

answers.A: Acute labyrinthitis
answers.B: Apical petrositis
answers.C: Bezold abscess
answers.D: Sigmoid sinus thrombosis
answers.E: Subperiosteal abscess

explanations.A: Labyrinthitis produces severe vertigo, nystagmus, tinnitus, and sensorineural hearing loss rather than an abduction deficit.
explanations.B: Extension of infection into the petrous apex produces Gradenigo syndrome, the triad of otitis media with otorrhea, deep facial or retro-orbital pain from CN V irritation, and diplopia from CN VI palsy.
explanations.C: A Bezold abscess presents as a tender neck mass deep to the sternocleidomastoid without cranial nerve findings.
explanations.D: Sigmoid sinus thrombosis causes spiking fevers, headache, and raised intracranial pressure rather than isolated abducens palsy with facial pain.
explanations.E: A subperiosteal abscess produces postauricular swelling and a protruding auricle, both of which are absent.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy with coalescent mastoiditis on intravenous antibiotics develops a new tender, fluctuant mass in the upper right neck that lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and extends toward the angle of the mandible. There is no postauricular swelling and no cranial nerve deficit. Contrast CT shows a rim-enhancing collection tracking inferiorly from the temporal bone. Which mechanism best explains this complication?

answers.A: Bone erosion through the lateral mastoid cortex beneath the periosteum
answers.B: Direct extension into the petrous apex of the temporal bone
answers.C: Erosion through the mastoid tip into the deep neck spaces
answers.D: Retrograde thrombophlebitis through mastoid emissary veins
answers.E: Toxin passage through the round window into the labyrinth

explanations.A: Erosion through the lateral cortex creates a subperiosteal abscess with visible postauricular swelling, which he does not have.
explanations.B: Petrous apex extension causes Gradenigo syndrome with retro-orbital pain and CN VI palsy rather than a neck mass.
explanations.C: A Bezold abscess forms when pus erodes through the thin medial mastoid tip and tracks along the sternocleidomastoid into the deep neck.
explanations.D: Retrograde thrombophlebitis via emissary veins produces sigmoid sinus thrombosis with spiking fevers and headache.
explanations.E: Toxin passage through the round window causes labyrinthitis with vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.question: An 11-year-old boy hospitalized for coalescent mastoiditis on intravenous antibiotics develops temperature spikes to 40 C occurring twice daily with intervening normal temperatures, along with severe headache and new papilledema on funduscopy. He has no neck stiffness, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows normal cell count, glucose, and protein with a negative Gram stain. There are no focal motor deficits. Which complication best accounts for his presentation?

answers.A: Acute suppurative labyrinthitis
answers.B: Bezold abscess of the deep neck
answers.C: Facial nerve palsy (CN VII)
answers.D: Purulent bacterial meningitis
answers.E: Sigmoid sinus thrombosis

explanations.A: Labyrinthitis causes vertigo, nystagmus, tinnitus, and hearing loss without picket-fence fevers or papilledema.
explanations.B: A Bezold abscess presents as a deep neck mass and does not raise intracranial pressure.
explanations.C: Facial nerve palsy from a dehiscent fallopian canal causes unilateral facial weakness alone.
explanations.D: Meningitis would produce nuchal rigidity with an abnormal cerebrospinal fluid profile, and his CSF is normal.
explanations.E: Retrograde thrombophlebitis from the mastoid into the sigmoid sinus produces spiking picket-fence fevers, headache, and obstructed venous drainage with elevated intracranial pressure and papilledema.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl being treated for acute otitis media develops the abrupt onset of severe spinning vertigo with vomiting. Examination shows spontaneous horizontal nystagmus and a markedly unsteady gait, and she reports new tinnitus. Audiometry shows new sensorineural hearing loss on the affected side. There is no facial weakness, no postauricular swelling, and no meningismus. Which mechanism best explains this complication?

answers.A: Bone erosion through the mastoid tip into the neck
answers.B: Dehiscence of the fallopian canal with nerve inflammation
answers.C: Ischemic necrosis of the tympanic membrane from pressure
answers.D: Passage of bacterial toxins through the round window
answers.E: Retrograde thrombophlebitis via mastoid emissary veins

explanations.A: Mastoid tip erosion produces a Bezold abscess in the deep neck without vestibular or cochlear symptoms.
explanations.B: A dehiscent fallopian canal exposes CN VII and causes facial palsy, which she does not have.
explanations.C: Pressure-induced ischemic necrosis of the tympanic membrane causes perforation with otorrhea and relief of pain, not vertigo with hearing loss.
explanations.D: Bacterial toxins and inflammatory mediators cross the round and oval windows into the inner ear, producing labyrinthitis with combined vestibular (vertigo, nystagmus) and cochlear (sensorineural loss, tinnitus) dysfunction.
explanations.E: Retrograde thrombophlebitis leads to sigmoid sinus thrombosis with fevers, headache, and raised intracranial pressure.

questions.question: Tympanocentesis is performed on a 3-year-old girl with severe acute otitis media and early mastoiditis who failed outpatient therapy. Laboratory results on the middle ear aspirate are shown. Which additional laboratory finding would be most consistent with this organism?

answers.A: Bile solubility with susceptibility to optochin
answers.B: Coagulase production with beta-hemolysis on blood agar
answers.C: Growth only on chocolate agar supplemented with factors V and X
answers.D: Oxidase positivity with colonies that slide intact across the agar
answers.E: Resistance to optochin with susceptibility to bacitracin

explanations.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae, the leading cause of acute otitis media and mastoiditis, is a catalase-negative alpha-hemolytic lancet-shaped diplococcus that is bile soluble and optochin sensitive.
explanations.B: Coagulase positivity with beta-hemolysis characterizes Staphylococcus aureus, which is catalase positive and appears in clusters rather than as lancet-shaped diplococci.
explanations.C: Dependence on factors V and X identifies Haemophilus influenzae, a gram-negative coccobacillus.
explanations.D: Oxidase positivity with hockey-puck colonies that slide across agar describes Moraxella catarrhalis, a gram-negative diplococcus.
explanations.E: Optochin resistance with bacitracin sensitivity would indicate Streptococcus pyogenes, which is beta-hemolytic rather than alpha-hemolytic.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy in full-time daycare presents with his fourth episode of acute otitis media this year, each occurring after a viral upper respiratory infection. His immunization record confirms four doses of the Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine. Tympanocentesis grows a gram-negative coccobacillus that grows only on chocolate agar, and the reference laboratory reports the isolate as nontypeable. Which best explains why his vaccination did not prevent this infection?

answers.A: Antigenic variation of the surface lipooligosaccharide
answers.B: Lack of the type b capsule targeted by the vaccine
answers.C: Production of beta-lactamase conferring ampicillin resistance
answers.D: Requirement for factors V and X that limits culture recovery
answers.E: Secretion of IgA protease that cleaves mucosal antibody

explanations.A: Lipooligosaccharide variation contributes to persistence but is not the reason the conjugate vaccine fails to cover this isolate.
explanations.B: The Hib conjugate vaccine targets the type b polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule, and nontypeable strains are unencapsulated, so vaccination confers no protection against them even though they are the H. influenzae strains that most commonly cause otitis media.
explanations.C: Beta-lactamase production explains failure of amoxicillin therapy rather than failure of vaccine-induced protection.
explanations.D: Growth requirements affect laboratory recovery, not host immunity or vaccine coverage.
explanations.E: IgA protease aids mucosal colonization but is not the vaccine target antigen.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl with acute otitis media has persistent fever and otalgia after 72 hours of high-dose amoxicillin. Tympanocentesis grows an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus whose colonies slide intact across the agar surface when pushed with a loop. The isolate is reported as beta-lactamase producing. Therapy is changed to ampicillin-sulbactam and she improves. Which best describes the contribution of sulbactam to this regimen?

answers.A: Blocks renal tubular secretion, prolonging the ampicillin half-life
answers.B: Enhances ampicillin entry through gram-negative porin channels
answers.C: Inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, halting protein synthesis
answers.D: Irreversibly inhibits bacterial beta-lactamase enzymes
answers.E: Prevents efflux pump extrusion of ampicillin from the cell

explanations.A: Blocking renal tubular secretion to prolong penicillin levels is the mechanism of probenecid, not sulbactam.
explanations.B: Sulbactam does not alter outer membrane porin permeability.
explanations.C: Ribosomal inhibition describes macrolides and other protein synthesis inhibitors, and sulbactam has no meaningful ribosomal activity.
explanations.D: Sulbactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor that irreversibly inactivates the enzyme, preventing degradation of ampicillin and restoring its activity against beta-lactamase producers such as Moraxella catarrhalis.
explanations.E: Efflux pump inhibition is not a mechanism of any clinically used beta-lactamase inhibitor.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman completes 10 days of intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam for complicated mastoiditis. Three days after finishing therapy she develops eight watery, foul-smelling stools daily with crampy lower abdominal pain and fever to 38.6 C. Her abdomen is diffusely tender without rebound or guarding, and there is no blood in the stool. Laboratory studies are shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Acute interstitial nephritis
answers.B: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
answers.C: Cholestatic hepatitis from drug injury
answers.D: Ischemic colitis from mesenteric hypoperfusion
answers.E: Pseudomembranous colitis from C. difficile

explanations.A: Beta-lactam interstitial nephritis presents with rash, fever, eosinophilia, and rising creatinine, and her renal function is normal.
explanations.B: Drug-induced hemolysis would cause anemia with jaundice and reticulocytosis rather than watery diarrhea and marked leukocytosis.
explanations.C: Ampicillin-sulbactam cholestatic hepatitis causes jaundice with elevated alkaline phosphatase and transaminases, not profuse diarrhea.
explanations.D: Ischemic colitis typically produces bloody diarrhea with sudden left-sided abdominal pain in a patient with vascular risk factors or hypotension.
explanations.E: Antibiotic-associated C. difficile colitis is a major adverse reaction of ampicillin-sulbactam and presents days after therapy with profuse watery diarrhea, fever, striking leukocytosis, and hypoalbuminemia.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy with acute mastoiditis is started on intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam. His parents ask how the antibiotic works. The ampicillin component is bactericidal and produces osmotic lysis of dividing organisms. Which action on the bacterial cell best accounts for this effect?

answers.A: Binding penicillin-binding proteins to block cross-linking
answers.B: Chelating divalent cations to destabilize the outer membrane
answers.C: Disrupting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV activity
answers.D: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase within the folate pathway
answers.E: Interfering with 30S ribosomal subunit initiation complexes

explanations.A: Ampicillin is a beta-lactam that binds penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking so the weakened cell wall fails and the organism lyses.
explanations.B: Divalent cation chelation destabilizing the outer membrane describes polymyxins.
explanations.C: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV inhibition is the mechanism of fluoroquinolones.
explanations.D: Dihydrofolate reductase inhibition describes trimethoprim, which is bacteriostatic through folate depletion.
explanations.E: Interference with 30S initiation complexes describes aminoglycosides and tetracyclines, which target protein synthesis rather than the cell wall.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy is newly diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, after evaluation confirmed symptoms present since kindergarten in both home and school settings. His parents ask why he developed the condition and whether anything they did caused it. He was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, and his mother did not smoke or drink. Which is the strongest known risk factor for ADHD?

answers.A: Exposure to artificial food dyes in early childhood
answers.B: Family history of ADHD in a first-degree relative
answers.C: High screen media use during the preschool years
answers.D: Maternal cigarette smoking during the pregnancy
answers.E: Preterm birth before 34 weeks of gestation

explanations.A: Dietary food dyes have been extensively studied and are not an established cause of ADHD.
explanations.B: ADHD is highly polygenic with heritability estimates of roughly 70% to 80%, making family history in a first-degree relative the single strongest risk factor.
explanations.C: Screen media use is associated with attention problems but has not been established as a strong causal risk factor.
explanations.D: Prenatal substance exposure including tobacco is a recognized risk factor but confers far less risk than genetic loading, and this mother did not smoke.
explanations.E: Prematurity is a recognized risk factor of modest magnitude, and this child was born at term.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy is evaluated for possible ADHD. His teacher documents 7 of 9 inattentive symptoms present consistently for the past 10 months, and his grades have fallen from B's to D's. His parents report no difficulty at home with homework, chores, play, or family outings, and his soccer coach has no concerns about his focus at practice. Symptoms were first noted at age 6. Psychotic and mood disorders have been excluded. Which DSM-5 criterion is not satisfied?

answers.A: Age of onset before 12 years
answers.B: Duration of at least 6 months
answers.C: Occurrence of symptoms in two or more settings
answers.D: Presence of six or more inattentive symptoms in total
answers.E: Significant impairment in functioning

explanations.A: Onset at age 6 satisfies the requirement that several symptoms be present before age 12.
explanations.B: A 10-month history exceeds the required 6-month persistence.
explanations.C: DSM-5 requires that several symptoms be present in two or more settings such as home, school, work, or social settings, and his symptoms occur only at school.
explanations.D: Seven inattentive symptoms exceeds the threshold of six required for children under 17.
explanations.E: A fall from B's to D's demonstrates clear interference with academic functioning.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, is started on atomoxetine because his family prefers a medication that is not a controlled substance. He has no cardiac history, and his baseline blood pressure and ECG are normal. Before starting, the physician counsels the family about the drug's boxed warning and arranges close follow-up during the first weeks of therapy. Which adverse effect is the subject of that boxed warning?

answers.A: Agranulocytosis
answers.B: Aplastic anemia
answers.C: Rebound hypertension after abrupt discontinuation
answers.D: Sudden cardiac death
answers.E: Suicidal ideation

explanations.A: Agranulocytosis is associated with clozapine and carbamazepine, not with atomoxetine.
explanations.B: Aplastic anemia is characteristic of carbamazepine and chloramphenicol rather than selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors.
explanations.C: Rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal is the warning for the alpha-2 agonists guanfacine and clonidine, which must be tapered.
explanations.D: Sudden cardiac death concerns arise with stimulants in patients with structural heart disease and are not the atomoxetine boxed warning.
explanations.E: Atomoxetine carries a boxed warning for suicidal ideation in children and adolescents, requiring close monitoring after initiation and dose changes.
